extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists and short-story authors) considering or working with multiple points of view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding whether to use single or multiple points of view and for structuring, pacing, worldbuilding, and characterization when using multiple POVs; includes a practical rewriting exercise (scene from another character's POV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide single POV vs multiple POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by asking yourself you want a single POV or multiple POVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some stories may not be served by multiple points of view; others benefit greatly. Choosing is intentional: you choose to use multiple POVs to let you dig into complexities if you want to. Consider implications for worldbuilding, pacing, and character before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple POVs to change worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilding can be changed the most by taking your story from single point of view to multiple points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple POVs allow you to show different facets of the world through different characters, revealing locations, institutions, or social details one character might miss or misinterpret. Examples referenced: books with alternating perspectives that reveal slowly (Meet Me in Another Life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple POVs to control pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple POVs are a good way to control your pacing; switching between POVs gives readers a chance to breathe and alters momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can have one plot moving faster and another slower to modulate tension (e.g., police procedurals using an A plot and B plot). Switching away from a highly tense scene to a slower POV releases pressure and makes the whole story feel deeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flesh out side characters and main characters via other POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple POVs provide a way to flesh out side characters, and even main characters, by looking at them from other sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing a character from another character's interior or exterior view can make them feel more real and important (example: TV adaptation of The Killing Floor / Reacher giving side characters POVs makes them feel more real). Use alternate POVs to make readers care about characters who previously felt peripheral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use POV shifts to examine and reveal motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple POVs can help examine motivations by letting you show characters' internal goals and reasoning that other characters can't see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jumping into another character's head (including an antagonist's) can complicate apparent black-and-white motivations and make their goals understandable. Example: Black Sun uses multiple POVs to illuminate motivations and make allegedly villainous actions more complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use POV choice to hide or reveal information
rubrics_metrics.description: Select which character's POV to use to control what the reader knows and when (e.g., hide information by withholding the POV of the character 'in the know').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary Robinette's heist example: not putting the character who knows key information in POV hides that information. Conversely, giving a character a POV reveals their knowledge. This is a tool for plotting, misdirection, and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use POV shift for shock or structural surprises
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden POV switch can be used deliberately for shock value or to create a structural surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary Robinette withheld a POV switch until a later book to use the shift for shock (making readers think the protagonist had died, then switching to the husband's POV). Timing and series context matter—doing the switch too early can blunt the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure ensemble narratives to manage multiple plot threads
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have an ensemble cast or multiple POVs, you gain the ability to manage A plot, B plot, C/D/E plots and thread them together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police procedurals are an example: devoting portions of POVs to B plots lets you balance multiple storylines. Multiple POVs let you tie threads together or keep them separate as needed to create depth and interlocking structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use POVs to manipulate clues and red herrings
rubrics_metrics.description: POV shifts can be used to change how readers perceive clues—turning obvious clues into red herrings or re-weighting their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching to a B-plot POV can make readers rethink the importance of a clue given in the A plot. This is a subtle pacing and mystery-crafting tool that is difficult to do without multiple POVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of emotional stakes and audience attachment from additional POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding POVs changes emotional stakes and audience attachment; giving a character POV increases audience investment and can change the series' emotional dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Reacher TV adaptation gave side characters POVs, increasing attachment and tension (we care more if they die). That also creates a cost in serialized work (readers may want to follow side characters in future installments), so consider long-term consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider medium differences (novel vs TV) when adding POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Medium can dictate or benefit from multiple POVs differently; adaptations may require more POVs to sustain episodic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Reacher example notes that TV structure demanded multiple POVs to fill episodes; what works in prose (single, intimate POV) may not translate to serialized visual media without structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show discrepancy between self-perception and external perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple POVs to show characters as they see themselves versus how others perceive them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing a character from the outside (another character's POV) can reveal contrasts with their inner self-assessment, adding complexity to characterization (example referenced: Black Sun's intersecting POVs).

rubrics_metrics.name: When rewriting a scene from another character's POV, keep the beats consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a scene in your current WIP from another character’s POV and keep the physical beats (actions) the same so you can explore the why without changing the scene's events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework guidance: keep the same beats (e.g., if a character pushes an old lady in a wheelchair down stairs, the action still happens) but make motivations and interiority make sense from the new POV. You may include details the original POV missed and can slightly extend the scene's start or end, but focus on digging into why the character behaves as they do.
